ITQAN (عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم): The same authority glosses التزكي throughout the Quran as Islam. ITQAN (أبو مالك): Abu Malik says وراء means “before” throughout the Quran, except in two verses where it means “other than.” | mentions 23:7, 4:24 ITQAN (أبو بكر بن عياش): Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash distinguishes the Quranic forms كسفا: one denotes punishment and the other a piece of cloud. ITQAN (عكرمة): ʿIkrima distinguishes what God made from what people made using two forms of سد. ITQAN (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak says every Quranic mention of a cup means wine. ITQAN (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak glosses فاطر in the Quran as Creator. ITQAN (سعيد بن جبير): Saʿid ibn Jubayr says every occurrence of إفك in the Quran means a lie. ITQAN (أبو العالية): Abu al-ʿAliya says Quranic commands to enjoin right mean Islam, while prohibitions of wrong mean worship of idols. ITQAN (مجاهد): Mujahid says the Quranic phrase إن الإنسان كفور refers to unbelievers. ITQAN (عمر بن عبد العزيز): ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz says every mention of abiding eternally means there is no repentance."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q01", "question": "What does 'Have you not seen' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression is explained by its knowledge/sight sense or its interrogative rhetorical force; these can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q01/p1", "position": "It calls Muhammad or the hearer to know the astonishing account with the certainty of inward sight or a reliable report.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr specify sight of the heart; Bursevī says God's report yields the certainty of sight; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the sight figurative. Dāmghānī compares 105:1 and 69:7."}, {"id": "2:258/q01/p2", "position": "The interrogative arrests attention, affirms the story, and invites amazement at the disputant's audacity.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Zajjāj, Wāḥidī, Rāzī, Qurtubī, and Ālūsī take its interrogative form as wonder or confirmation; Burhān likens it to an alerting command."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q02", "question": "How is 'Have you not seen' read?", "turns_on": "The final rāʾ's vowel in connected recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q02/p1", "position": "ʿAlī reads the final rāʾ with sukūn, dropping the yāʾ or carrying pause pronunciation into connection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurtubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Samīn transmit it; Samīn recalls its analysis at 2:243."}, {"id": "2:258/q02/p2", "position": "The majority vocalize the final rāʾ in connected speech.", "reasons": "Qurtubī contrasts this with ʿAlī's pausal/jussive form."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q03", "question": "What does the address imply about Muhammad's knowledge of earlier history?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q03/p1", "position": "His knowledge of this earlier episode must come from revelation, confirming his prophethood.", "reasons": "Zajjāj argues that the unlettered Muhammad had neither learned the Torah and Gospel nor had a human teacher, excluding the other proposed sources."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q04", "question": "What note is made about the earlier wording 'Have you not seen'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q04/p1", "position": "Its wording and analysis were discussed already at parallel occurrences.", "reasons": "Samīn refers to 2:243; Abū Ḥayyān says he does not repeat his earlier treatment."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q05", "question": "What does the preposition in 'Have you seen to the one' do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q05/p1", "position": "It is Arabic idiom for directing attention in wonder to such a remarkable person.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ gives Arab usage; Wāḥidī says sight reaches an extraordinary endpoint; Ṭabrisī likens it to a comparison marker."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q06", "question": "Who disputed with Abraham?", "turns_on": "Whether the extra-Qur'anic identification as Nimrod can be relied on.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q06/p1", "position": "The disputant was Nimrod, the Babylonian king and claimant to divinity.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and many early transmitters name him; reports vary on his ancestry. Study Quran says the name rests on folklore and no hadith names him, though it reports the identification."}, {"id": "2:258/q06/p2", "position": "The verse leaves the antagonist unnamed; the traditional Nimrod identification is uncertain.", "reasons": "Study Quran observes that no hadith names him and the biblical account is ambiguous."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q07", "question": "What ancestry and status are reported for Nimrod?", "turns_on": "The competing genealogies and historical descriptions in transmitted accounts.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q07/p1", "position": "He was the first tyrant, claimed divinity, wore a crown, and owned or built Babylon's tower.", "reasons": "Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ, and later sources transmit the tower and tyranny; Muqātil also calls him earth's first ruler."}, {"id": "2:258/q07/p2", "position": "Four people ruled the world: believing Solomon and Dhū al-Qarnayn, unbelieving Nimrod and Nebuchadnezzar.", "reasons": "Mujāhid or Ibn ʿAbbās transmit this list; Ibn Kathīr adds 'God knows best'; Bursevī gives an additional identification of Nebuchadnezzar with Shaddād."}, {"id": "2:258/q07/p3", "position": "He descends through Canaan and Cush; reports vary in their intermediate names and order.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurtubī, Ibn Kathīr, and Ālūsī transmit differing Canaan/Cush/Shem or Ham lines; the variation does not change the identity."}, {"id": "2:258/q07/p4", "position": "He descends through Falikh or Faligh, Eber/ʿĀbir, Shalikh and Arfakhshadh to Shem.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī gives the short Falikh line; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurtubī, and Ibn Kathīr expand it."}, {"id": "2:258/q07/p5", "position": "He was the first king on earth.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj and some reports say so; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the claim and Qurtubī and Abū Ḥayyān repeat his objection."}, {"id": "2:258/q07/p6", "position": "Nimrod the elder ruled four hundred years; a separate younger Nimrod ruled one year.", "reasons": "Qurtubī transmits this distinction; Ibn Kathīr also mentions four hundred years for the tyrant."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q08", "question": "What inward reading is given to Nimrod and his kingdom?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q08/p1", "position": "Nimrod can symbolize the commanding soul, his kingdom bodily powers and the lower world, and Abraham the sacred spirit.", "reasons": "Ālūsī allows this alongside the historical account; he reads Nimrod's life-and-death boast as turning powers toward pleasure or restraining them."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q09", "question": "What other historical comparison is reported beside Nimrod?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q09/p1", "position": "The tyrant al-Ḍaḥḥāk was killed by Afrīdūn; reports differ on his lineage and associate him with Nimrod or with a distinct earlier ruler.", "reasons": "Qurtubī says he ruled a thousand years and first crucified and amputated; Abū Ḥayyān relays al-Suhaylī and Abū Tammām's poetic comparison; Qurtubī also gives al-Suhaylī's separate lineage."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q10", "question": "What does 'disputed' mean and what was the dispute about?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is the verb's reciprocal force or the precise claim contested.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q10/p1", "position": "Ḥājja means to contend by proof and counterproof, seeking to prevail over the other.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya derives the reciprocal form from ḥujja; Ṭabāṭabāʾī traces ḥujja to intention. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes the form lacks a known simple stem and commonly implies contentious, even false, disputation."}, {"id": "2:258/q10/p2", "position": "They argued over Abraham's Lord, His existence and exclusive right to be worshipped, against the king's claim of divinity.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr compares Pharaoh at 28:38; Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees a contest over exclusive lordship within a culture that admitted other gods."}, {"id": "2:258/q10/p3", "position": "The king presented a false argument as though it were proof.", "reasons": "Ālūsī explains why the verse still calls the exchange disputation; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes the verb often denotes contentious false debate."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q11", "question": "When and where did the debate happen?", "turns_on": "The reported chronology relative to the idols and fire, and the grain-rationing setting.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q11/p1", "position": "It followed the breaking of idols and preceded Abraham's being thrown into the fire; Nimrod imprisoned and questioned him.", "reasons": "Muqātil's account has Nimrod release Abraham for burning; al-Ṣādiq alternatively places the dispute before the idols were broken."}, {"id": "2:258/q11/p2", "position": "It occurred after Abraham survived the fire.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī and others place it then, often at the food-distribution court; Ālūsī transmits an al-Ṣādiq report to this effect, conflicting with Ṭabrisī's other attribution."}, {"id": "2:258/q11/p3", "position": "The debate was at Nimrod's food court, where visitors had to acknowledge him as lord to obtain grain.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd locates Nimrod at Mosul; reports say he refused Abraham food after the exc

hange."}, {"id": "2:258/q11/p4", "position": "One al-Ṣādiq report places it before the idols were broken and before the fire.", "reasons": "This differs from Muqātil's and another al-Ṣādiq chronology."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q12", "question": "What provision reached Abraham after Nimrod denied him food?", "turns_on": "The reported material brought home and the resulting food.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q12/p1", "position": "Sand or earth carried home in sacks became fine flour or food for his household.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says Sarah found fine grain or flour and Abraham recognized God's provision; accounts vary whether he brought sand to comfort or distract the children."}, {"id": "2:258/q12/p2", "position": "Red earth became red wheat, whose grain grew densely along the stalk.", "reasons": "Abū Ṣāliḥ's report via Ibn Abī Shayba gives this specific variant."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q13", "question": "What prior culture and beliefs frame the king's claim?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q13/p1", "position": "People became attached to sensory idols and intermediary gods; powerful rulers exploited their visible authority to claim superior divinity.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī discusses innate awareness of higher powers, divergent planetary cults, and Pharaoh's claim of supremacy while recognizing other gods."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q14", "question": "How are Abraham's name and the nearby yāʾ read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q14/p1", "position": "The name has a canonical dialectal form Ibrāhām, with long ā replacing ī; the three instances follow the same variant.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER notes Arabization of the Hebrew name and no difference in reference."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q15", "question": "Whose Lord is meant by 'his Lord'?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of the pronoun; several commentators allow both.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q15/p1", "position": "It is Abraham's Lord.", "reasons": "Rāzī compares 6:80; Ṭabāṭabāʾī points to Abraham's later words 'my Lord'; Bursevī and Ālūsī see an honorific assurance of divine support."}, {"id": "2:258/q15/p2", "position": "It can refer to the disputant's Lord, the same God who is Abraham's Lord.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Nasafī, Biqāʿī, and Samīn admit the grammatical possibility."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q16", "question": "How does the grant of kingship relate to the dispute?", "turns_on": "Causal lām versus a temporal interpretation of an and whether the grant and dispute were simultaneous.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q16/p1", "position": "The clause is causal: kingship led Nimrod to arrogance and disputation.", "reasons": "Qurtubī and Samīn analyze an omitted causal lām; Ālūsī prefers causation over a strained temporal reading; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says naming the divine favor exposes ingratitude."}, {"id": "2:258/q16/p2", "position": "The phrase highlights Nimrod's perverse ingratitude: he repaid God's favor with opposition.", "reasons": "Kashshāf and Bayḍāwī compare 56:82; Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites the Sanmar poem and 28:8 for ironic reversal."}, {"id": "2:258/q16/p3", "position": "The clause is temporal: he disputed when God gave him kingship.", "reasons": "Kashshāf allows an as a time expression; Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, and Ālūsī object that the grant and debate were not simultaneous unless the time is extended."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q17", "question": "What is the grammatical status of 'because God granted him kingship'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q17/p1", "position": "It is accusative under an understood causal lām; a causal clause with distinct agents may also be genitive after deletion of the preposition.", "reasons": "Qurtubī gives the accusative analysis; Samīn gives both case possibilities and explains why it is not a same-agent purpose object; Ālūsī agrees."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q18", "question": "Who received the kingship?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of ātāhu, the meaning of mulk, and whether God grants worldly rule to an unbeliever.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q18/p1", "position": "God gave worldly kingship to the disputant Nimrod.", "reasons": "Zajjāj says the opponent displayed a king's power while Abraham was a prophet; Rāzī cites majority reports and the arrogance implied by the grant; Ālūsī cites early tradition; Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites Nimrod's visible sovereignty."}, {"id": "2:258/q18/p2", "position": "God gave Abraham kingship, understood as prophetic or lawful authority.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥudhayfa, al-Mahdawī, Abū al-Qāsim al-Balkhī, and others invoke 2:124 and 4:54 or argue God would not give binding authority to an unbeliever; Rāzī notes the nearest-antecedent argument. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ālūsī reject this as forced or contrary to the reports."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q19", "question": "Why is God explicitly named in the grant and sun challenge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q19/p1", "position": "The explicit divine name shifts from a pronoun or 'my Lord' to assert God's lordship over both disputants and block Nimrod's verbal misapplication.", "reasons": "Ālūsī notes the pronoun-to-name shift and its reply to Nimrod's 'I'; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it prevents the king from reusing Abraham's 'my Lord' wording."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q20", "question": "Why does Nimrod's sovereignty make Abraham's stance striking?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q20/p1", "position": "Abraham publicly confronted a powerful unbelieving sovereign while himself lacking the king's worldly power.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this as a reason to identify Nimrod as recipient of kingship; al-Aṣamm says a kingly Abraham would have stopped Nimrod's killing, but the Qāḍī replies spiritual and coercive powers can coexist."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q21", "question": "What kind of kingship may God give an unbeliever?", "turns_on": "Whether mulk means factual control or rightful religious authority, and whether Nimrod was an unbeliever when granted it.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q21/p1", "position": "Worldly sovereignty, wealth, followers, and coercive power may be given to a disbeliever; it can be a trial.", "reasons": "Zajjāj cites 3:26; Jishumī and Ṭabrisī distinguish worldly dominion from rightful command; Ālūsī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī say this still is God's grant. Bursevī challenges the Muʿtazilite aṣlaḥ doctrine."}, {"id": "2:258/q21/p2", "position": "Binding, rightful kingship and obligatory obedience cannot be granted to a known corrupter.", "reasons": "Abū al-Qāsim al-Balkhī and some Imāmīs cite divine covenant and separate rightful authority from Nimrod's coercion; Abū Ḥayyān says spiritual authority can coexist with an oppressor's political power."}, {"id": "2:258/q21/p3", "position": "Nimrod may have received rule while a believer and later disbelieved.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim and Rāzī present this as a way to reconcile the grant with later unbelief."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q22", "question": "What does the episode teach rulers about sovereignty?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q22/p1", "position": "Sovereignty is a divine trust or deputyship; gratitude and justice preserve it, while arrogant claims to divinity ruin ruler and subjects.", "reasons": "Elmalılı contrasts Nimrod with David and Solomon, says power is a trial, and warns that changing truth and ruling by desire lead to destruction. Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats kingship as a divinely bestowed capacity that can be rightly or wrongly used."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q23", "question": "What answer is given to the claim that Abraham's family received kingship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q23/p1", "position": "The cited grant to Abraham's family does not prove Abraham personally ruled.", "reasons": "Rāzī replies to use of 4:54 for the Abraham-pronoun reading."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q24", "question": "How is 'when Abraham said' attached syntactically?", "turns_on": "The syntactic governor of idh and whether the two time clauses can be appositional.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q24/p1", "position": "The time clause is governed by ḥājja: the disputation happened when Abraham spoke.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, Bursevī, and Ālūsī support this; Samīn calls it clearest."}, {"id": "2:258/q24/p2", "position": "It depends on ātāhu or substitutes for the preceding grant clause as a time expression.", "reasons": "Kashshāf and Abū al-Baqāʾ propose this; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn object that the two events have different times; Abū al-Baqāʾ conditions it on a temporal, rather than causal, an."}, {"id": "2:258/q24/p3", "position": "It depends on 'have you seen'.", "reasons": "Makkī's proposal is rejected by Samīn since the seeing did not occur at the time Abraham spoke."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q25", "question": "What unstated speech prompts Abraham's reply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q25/p1", "position": "The king first asked Abraham, 'Who is your Lord?' and the question is omitted because Abraham's answer makes it clear.", "reasons": "Rāzī compares Moses and Pharaoh in 43:46 and 26:23; Biqāʿī infers an earlier exchange and claim of shared lordship."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q26", "question": "How is 'my Lord, the one who gives life and death' parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q26/p1", "position": "Rabbī is the subject and its relative clause the predicate; the whole assertion is the object of 'said'.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn give the clause analysis; Samīn also parses ana uḥyī analogously."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q27", "question": "Why use a relative clause for God's action but a finite clause for the king's?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording marks a mere shared claim or Nimrod's claim of exclusive lordship.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q27/p1", "position": "The relative predicate marks God's exclusive possession of life and death; Nimrod's bare verb avoids claiming explicit exclusivity.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn say the king could not claim that none other gives life and death, though Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads his reply as claiming exclusive lordship."}, {"id": "2:258/q27/p2", "position": "The king

's uncoordinated 'I' asserts that he himself is the Lord Abraham described, claiming supremacy rather than partnership.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads the absence of a conjunction and omission of other gods as signs of this aim."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q28", "question": "How is 'my Lord' read?", "turns_on": "The vowel or sukūn on the first-person yāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q28/p1", "position": "The yāʾ is quiescent, giving rabbī; Ḥamza and al-Aʿmash are named.", "reasons": "Thalabī, Baghawī, Nashr, and others transmit it; Baghawī lists parallel yāʾ contexts."}, {"id": "2:258/q28/p2", "position": "The yāʾ is pronounced with fatḥa in rabbiya before the following article; this is the common reading.", "reasons": "Jishumī relates the opening to the following alif; Qiraat-ER calls it the more emphatic declaration."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q29", "question": "How does Abraham's opening function as correction of Nimrod's claim?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q29/p1", "position": "It reverses Nimrod's mistaken attribution of life and death to himself.", "reasons": "Itqān classifies this as qasr qalb, correction of a reversed attribution."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q30", "question": "What does God's giving life and death mean?", "turns_on": "The scope of life and death: origination generally, animal life, or resurrection in particular.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q30/p1", "position": "God actually originates life and death in bodies, creates beings after nonexistence, and can restore the dead.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says He gives and takes life by will; Rāzī argues that changing life and death require a freely acting creator, not a fixed necessary cause; Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses conscious animal life; Elmalılı includes resurrection."}, {"id": "2:258/q30/p2", "position": "The divine act includes giving life by resurrection and death after a former life.", "reasons": "Baghawī says Abraham's first proof concerned resurrection; Tustarī's surrounding readings connect direct witnessing of revival to certainty."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q31", "question": "Why mention life before death and choose it as the first sign?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q31/p1", "position": "Life is the first foundational blessing and a particularly clear sign of the Creator.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī stresses life as the first favor and death without bodily injury; Jishumī says the sign recalls divine unity and favor; Rāzī says life's observable marvels outnumber death's, comparing 2:28, 67:2, 26:81."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q32", "question": "Are the objects of 'gives life and death' deliberately omitted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q32/p1", "position": "Yes; the focus is God's power itself, not particular recipients.", "reasons": "Burhān compares Moses' question about idols that neither hear nor see."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q33", "question": "What is the point of naming life and death as signs of God?", "turns_on": "The kind of inference drawn from divine acts and the relative force of the two signs.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q33/p1", "position": "Acts no creature can originate are the way to infer a freely acting Creator, and life is an especially clear instance.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues contingent changes and diverse animal forms cannot proceed from an unchanging necessary cause; Jishumī and Ṭabrisī infer God from unique acts; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says innate awareness of superior powers survives human neglect."}, {"id": "2:258/q33/p2", "position": "Creating life is stronger evidence than altering the sun's course, though unjust observers trivialize it.", "reasons": "Elmalılı distinguishes the strength of the sign from audience response."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q34", "question": "Was Nimrod's killing-and-sparing actually performed in the Qur'anic account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q34/p1", "position": "The verse reports his claim but does not state that he carried out the killing and sparing.", "reasons": "Rāzī distinguishes the Qur'anic wording from the extra-Qur'anic staging reports."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q35", "question": "Why might Abraham leave the first false claim unanswered?", "turns_on": "Whether silence communicates the obviousness of the fallacy or leaves a public doubt.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q35/p1", "position": "Its falsehood was obvious, so an immediate verbal refutation was unnecessary.", "reasons": "Bursevī and Ālūsī say the equivocation did not deserve prolonged response; Rāzī objects that leaving a seemingly damaging doubt unanswered could confuse an audience."}, {"id": "2:258/q35/p2", "position": "A visible objection should be answered at once to avoid making the prophet appear defeated.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the apparent shift might concede weakness; Ālūsī reports and rejects that concern."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q36", "question": "What did Nimrod mean by 'I give life and cause death'?", "turns_on": "Whether the king merely played on the terms, staged starvation, invoked mediated causes, or claimed real divine agency.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q36/p1", "position": "He killed one person and spared or pardoned another, equivocating between preservation and creative life.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Qatāda, Mujāhid, and most commentators report this. Ṭabarī cites 5:32 for calling saving a person 'giving life'; Rāzī and Ibn Kathīr reject it as a genuine answer, while it remains their reported claim."}, {"id": "2:258/q36/p2", "position": "He starved four captives, fed two to preserve their lives, and let two die.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī's account is repeated by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurtubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Durr; the number four differentiates it from the two-person execution account."}, {"id": "2:258/q36/p3", "position": "He claimed actual, even delegated, divine power over life and death and asserted that he was Abraham's lord.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr rejects treating the pardon story as a real rebuttal; Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees a claim to superior lordship, while Ālūsī considers delegated planetary or creative power."}, {"id": "2:258/q36/p4", "position": "He meant that intercourse and depositing sperm give life, while killing gives death.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān transmits this third explanation."}, {"id": "2:258/q36/p5", "position": "He objected that life and death arise through earthly and celestial causes, while humans also cause them indirectly by sex or poison.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this reconstruction over the ordinary pardon and execution report; he says Abraham's solar reply shows who controls the celestial mediators."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q37", "question": "How is 'I' read and what is its alif?", "turns_on": "Whether the connected alif is omitted, retained by a transmitted dialect, or analyzed as an original pronoun letter.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q37/p1", "position": "Most readers omit the alif in connected speech and retain it at pause; its alif marks the pausal vowel.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī likens it to pausal hāʾ and hamzat al-waṣl; Wāḥidī and Rāzī prefer omission. Qurtubī adds Basran and Jawharī analyses."}, {"id": "2:258/q37/p2", "position": "Nāfiʿ or Medinan readers retain and lengthen the alif before a following open or rounded hamza in connected speech; reports differ on kasra and exceptions.", "reasons": "Fārisī names Warsh, Qālūn, Ibn Abī Uways and exclusions such as 26:15; Qurtubī notes 7:188; Abū Ḥayyān records a kasra-hamza report. Wāḥidī and al-Naḥḥās object."}, {"id": "2:258/q37/p3", "position": "The retained alif represents a Banū Tamīm dialect, not an illegitimate pause form carried into liaison.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn prefer the dialect account; Wāḥidī considers liaison retention only a poetic necessity, citing al-Aʿshā, al-Kisāʾī, and another poem."}, {"id": "2:258/q37/p4", "position": "The Kufans treat the alif as part of the full pronoun; others delete it for lightness.", "reasons": "Qurtubī contrasts this with the Basran account of extra pausal alif; Samīn gives other pronoun forms an, anā, and ān."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q38", "question": "What other nuance is given to the king's claim?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q38/p1", "position": "He may have claimed capacity for every divine action, inviting Abraham to find one he could not perform.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī reports this scope of his boast, which the solar course refutes."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q39", "question": "Why did Abraham use the sun challenge after the life-and-death exchange?", "turns_on": "Whether Abraham changes proofs, changes examples, completes a mediated-cause proof, or makes an integrated argument about creation and governance.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q39/p1", "position": "He moved to a second, clearer proof that the king could not evade or confuse.", "reasons": "Zajjāj says it silenced him concisely; legal theorists distinguish literal creation from Nimrod's figurative evasion; al-Kashshāf, al-Baghawī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Kuranyolu stress clarity before the audience. Al-Rāzī objects that an unanswered challenge might imply weakness."}, {"id": "2:258/q39/p2", "position": "He kept one proof but replaced its example: only God can do acts beyond human power.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabrisī say a second illustration reinforces an already sound case; Rāzī's investigators say life and celestial motion are two examples of the same inference; Bayḍāwī and Bursevī stress continuity."}, {"id": "2:258/q39/p3", "position": "Abraham first challenged Nimrod to revive the man he killed, then added the sun challenge.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣādiq and another report give an explicit intervening refutation; Ālūsī says the Qur'an omits it because the falsity is obvious."}, {"id": "2:258/q39/p4", "position": "The solar motion completes the original proof because God directs celestial causes that mediate life and death.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this reconstruction: humans can cause effects indirectly but cannot command heavenly motions; Ālūsī reports and challenges it as unsupported by t

he wording."}, {"id": "2:258/q39/p5", "position": "The sun was chosen because Nimrod's hearers revered it as a god.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports this explanation; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says even on that belief its motion depends on the Lord of lords."}, {"id": "2:258/q39/p6", "position": "The two statements form one proof against dividing original creation from ongoing governance.", "reasons": "Ālūsī says a dependent Nimrod cannot gain independent creative power later; the sun's continuing motion and origination require the same Creator."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q40", "question": "How does the fāʾ before 'God brings the sun' work?", "turns_on": "Whether the conjunction signals an ellipted condition or a general connection.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q40/p1", "position": "It answers an omitted condition: if Nimrod claims this power, then God brings the sun as stated.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn note that an ordinary quotation after 'Abraham said' would lack the fāʾ; Ālūsī says it follows from Nimrod's sophistry."}, {"id": "2:258/q40/p2", "position": "It simply connects the reply to the preceding claim.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ frames Nimrod's confused assertion as the occasion for the new proof."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q41", "question": "What does the sun challenge prove?", "turns_on": "The force assigned to the westward-sun demand and its eschatological extension.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q41/p1", "position": "The real Lord governs the sun; a claimant to comparable divinity must reverse its rising, which Nimrod cannot do.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī states the demand conditionally; Ibn Kathīr joins control of life with heavenly bodies; al-Biqāʿī notes the sun rose long before Nimrod; Ālūsī calls the imperative an incapacitating challenge."}, {"id": "2:258/q41/p2", "position": "It establishes one freely acting Lord for both human life and celestial motion, anticipating the sun's eventual westward rising.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥarālī reads the body's soul as its sun and links the final reversal to the Hour; Muqātil and Qurtubī report God's promise of the westward sunrise."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q42", "question": "How are the sun's movement and its directions constructed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the prepositional directions attach to the verbs or to omitted circumstantial descriptors.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q42/p1", "position": "The bāʾ makes 'comes' transitive as 'brings'; each min phrase marks the place from which the sun starts.", "reasons": "Samīn contrasts 'the sun came' with 'God brought it'; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī likewise take min as source."}, {"id": "2:258/q42/p2", "position": "Each directional phrase may modify an omitted circumstance, 'subjugated' or 'obedient'.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ allows it but Samīn criticizes his reversal; Ālūsī reports it as an alternative."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q43", "question": "What other readings of nearby yāʾs are recorded?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q43/p1", "position": "The written yāʾ of 'God brings the sun' is consistently retained by codices and readers; other first-person yāʾ examples show different pause or vowel conventions.", "reasons": "Nashr lists fifteen agreed written yāʾs including this phrase, fourteen disputed yāʾs which Ḥamza sukunizes, and eighteen agreed-open yāʾs; Qunbul has two transmitted pause forms in another case."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q44", "question": "What does the sun's forced motion illustrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q44/p1", "position": "God compels the sun against its apparent natural course; Nimrod would have to reverse that imposed motion.", "reasons": "Nasafī compares an ant walking on a millstone while water carries it the opposite way."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q45", "question": "What does the sun's being feminine contribute to its wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q45/p1", "position": "Shams is grammatically feminine, with plural shumūs; its Qur'anic agreement remains feminine regardless of claims about ancient solar deities or Abraham's language.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives the lexical gender; Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects using an alleged male sun-god and Anunit or an ungendered Syriac original to overturn the Arabic grammar."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q46", "question": "What inward reading is given to the sun challenge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q46/p1", "position": "The sun can signify gnosis rising from its eastern source; the westward demand tests the soul or evokes the spirit's return after setting in the body.", "reasons": "Ālūsī offers these alternatives."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q47", "question": "What ancillary point is made about imagery of sun, day, and night?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q47/p1", "position": "Comparing a benefaction to the sun mainly conveys universality, with comfort and brightness as possible further associations.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir says al-Nābigha's daytime line expects night afterward; a beloved may be called one's day and night, while calling a praised person's anger 'night' directly is disliked because of its darkness."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q48", "question": "Why could Nimrod not counter by claiming the eastern sunrise or demanding a western sunrise from God?", "turns_on": "Whether his silence was divinely imposed, based on knowledge and fear, obvious to the public, or an objection to the reconstruction.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q48/p1", "position": "God deprived him of that reply to support Abraham and establish a sign.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Baghawī, Rāzī, and Nasafī transmit this; Baghawī prefers it. Ālūsī calls the forgetfulness explanation weak."}, {"id": "2:258/q48/p2", "position": "He knew from Abraham's survival of the fire or other signs that God could reverse the sun, and feared added disgrace.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Rāzī, Baghawī, and Ṭabrisī give this reason."}, {"id": "2:258/q48/p3", "position": "The crowd knew the sun rose before Nimrod; a claim to cause its regular rising would plainly be false.", "reasons": "Legal theorists and Qurtubī say the audience would call him a liar; Abū Ḥayyān says he knew he could not reverse it."}, {"id": "2:258/q48/p4", "position": "The supposed counterchallenge exposes a weakness in the familiar reconstruction of the debate.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues that waiting for a westward sunrise would replace the original proof and leave Abraham's silence unexplained; Ālūsī replies the objection also presses Rāzī's version."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q49", "question": "What does 'he was confounded' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the context uses the core sense of false accusation or the resulting sense of stunned silence.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q49/p1", "position": "He became stunned, perplexed, speechless, and lost his argument.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī distinguishes bewilderment from false accusation; Wāḥidī quotes ʿUrwa's verse; al-Biqāʿī derives a frozen state; most later interpreters treat it as defeat by proof."}, {"id": "2:258/q49/p2", "position": "The root can mean confronting someone with a lie or slander, from which bewilderment is figuratively extended.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Ṭabrisī explain the semantic shift; Jishumī and Samīn cite a Prophetic description of Jews as people of falsehood; Tabrisī compares 4:20."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q50", "question": "How is 'he was confounded' read and who is its subject?", "turns_on": "Vowels of the verb, transitivity, and whether Abraham or Nimrod functions as agent.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q50/p1", "position": "The majority read passive buhita; the disbeliever is the passive subject, with Abraham or his speech the understood agent.", "reasons": "Akhfash calls this common; Samīn gives the syntactic analysis; Ibn Jinnī notes the related intensive faʿula form."}, {"id": "2:258/q50/p2", "position": "With fatḥa on bāʾ and hāʾ, Abraham actively confounded the unbeliever.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ, Nuʿaym, Abū Razīn and others are cited; the relative pronoun becomes accusative. Thaʿlabī adduces 21:97. Some allow the same vowels intransitively."}, {"id": "2:258/q50/p3", "position": "With fatḥa on bāʾ and ḍamma on hāʾ, the disbeliever is the intransitive subject, intensely bewildered.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī prefers its intensifying faʿula morphology and cites a forceful-striking usage; Abū Ḥaywa and others transmit it."}, {"id": "2:258/q50/p4", "position": "A form with kasra on hāʾ, like ʿalima or dahisha, also means he became bewildered.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash reports it; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurtubī, Samīn, and Ālūsī mention it among four forms."}, {"id": "2:258/q50/p5", "position": "The active reading can mean the defeated Nimrod insulted or falsely accused Abraham.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurtubī transmit this alternative; Ibn Jinnī says he may have tried to confound Abraham but failed."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q51", "question": "What happened when Nimrod's argument was defeated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q51/p1", "position": "In one account, Nimrod resorted to ordering Abraham burned.", "reasons": "Qurtubī comments that tyrants use punishment when they lose argument and God saved Abraham."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q52", "question": "Why call the opponent 'the one who disbelieved'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q52/p1", "position": "The relative description explains his defeat by naming his disbelief as the cause, and marks his disputation itself as disbelief.", "reasons": "Bursevī stresses the causal implication; al-Biqāʿī says it exposes denial of God's exclusive power."}]}

{"id": "2:258/q54", "question": "What is the grammatical role of 'the one who disbelieved'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q54/p1", "position": "It is nominative as the verb's subject or passive subject, depending on the reading.", "reasons": "Jishumī treats it as nominative by its relation to the verb; Samīn gives the passive-subject analysis."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q55", "question": "What does 'God does not guide the wrongdoing people' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the withheld guidance concerns argument, enabling aid, faith, or the afterlife, and whom 'wrongdoers' includes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q55/p1", "position": "He does not guide them to a valid proof or successful argument against truth.", "reasons": "Muqātil links the statement to Nimrod and 9:19; al-Ṭabarī says falsehood has no prevailing argument; Rāzī rejects saying there is a valid argument for unbelief that God withholds."}, {"id": "2:258/q55/p2", "position": "He does not lead persistent wrongdoers to faith and truth; their injustice blocks their benefit from clear proof.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this contextual account and cites 6:111; Abū Ḥayyān prefers those decreed to persist in unbelief; Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes injustice the cause of withholding guidance, not the effect. Al-Suddī explicitly says faith."}, {"id": "2:258/q55/p3", "position": "He does not assist their corrupt ends or give them enabling grace and success.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Nasafī, and Bayḍāwī present this sense; Rāzī rejects a version that says God withholds a rationally impossible favor."}, {"id": "2:258/q55/p4", "position": "He does not guide them to Paradise or save them from punishment.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Bayḍāwī, Bursevī and Ālūsī report this; Rāzī rejects it as distant from the debate context."}, {"id": "2:258/q55/p5", "position": "The general wording particularly concerns unbelievers or those who die unjust; it does not deny guidance to repentant wrongdoers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya limits the warning in light of possible repentance; Ṭabrisī distinguishes general and believer-specific senses of guidance, comparing 41:17; Abū Ḥayyān restricts it to decreed persistence."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q56", "question": "What does the verse imply about divine success or punishment after the debate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q56/p1", "position": "The proof prevailed but God did not inspire the wrongdoer to accept it; his false argument and punishment follow.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr stresses invalid proof and divine anger; Elmalılı says acceptance of truth would have prevented the darkness."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q57", "question": "How does divine guidance operate when injustice obstructs it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q57/p1", "position": "God guides every creature through real causal paths to its ends; injustice substitutes false paths and so fails.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares 20:50 and 11:56, fire and plant growth, education, corrupt offices, and the eventual exposure of false acts; truth endures while imitation fails."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q58", "question": "Does God’s lack of guidance here conflict with guidance given elsewhere to wrongdoers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q58/p1", "position": "No; guidance has general and special senses, and guidance toward a path differs from aid to follow it or entry to Paradise.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī compares the guidance of Thamūd at 41:17 and his discussion at 2:26; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds that a wrongdoer can repent."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q59", "question": "Why is the final denial of guidance so concise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q59/p1", "position": "Its short general form applies beyond Nimrod and conveys more meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī cites al-Imām for the rhetorical force of brevity."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q60", "question": "Who are 'the wrongdoing people' in this verse?", "turns_on": "Specific unbelief versus the broader pattern of injustice.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q60/p1", "position": "It points first to Nimrod or disbelievers who deny God's power.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies Nimrod; Ibn al-Jawzī equates wrongdoers with unbelievers; al-Biqāʿī includes wrongful killing and sparing."}, {"id": "2:258/q60/p2", "position": "It applies generally to those who turn from truth toward falsehood and put things out of place.", "reasons": "Māwardī gives the broader sense; al-Ṭabarī calls such denial self-wronging; Ṭabāṭabāʾī defines injustice by deviation from proper action."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q61", "question": "What does this debate establish about religious argument?", "turns_on": "The status, conditions, and epistemic implications of religious disputation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q61/p1", "position": "Reasoned disputation and adducing proof are permissible, and may be required to call others to truth.", "reasons": "Qurtubī cites 2:111, 10:68, 21:52, 11:32-35, 3:61 and 3:66, plus Prophetic and Companion debates; Nasafī says prophets cannot perform forbidden debate; Jishumī and Ṭabrisī use it against blind imitation."}, {"id": "2:258/q61/p2", "position": "The argument validates inference and shows knowledge of God is acquired rather than innate necessity.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabrisī say a debate over a necessary truth would be pointless; it refutes blind imitation. Ṭabāṭabāʾī separately says innate disposition points people to a maker."}, {"id": "2:258/q61/p3", "position": "Debate should seek God's approval and accept the truth that appears.", "reasons": "Al-Muzanī states this condition; another view says usefulness also depends on comparable religion, reason, understanding and fairness."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q62", "question": "How does this episode relate to the preceding verse about divine guardianship?", "turns_on": "Whether the episode illustrates both sides of 2:257 or chiefly the disbeliever's side.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q62/p1", "position": "It illustrates God guiding and supporting Abraham, His ally, and leaving the unbelieving ally of false powers confounded.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Elmalılı and Ṭabāṭabāʾī connect it to 2:257; Abū Ḥayyān compares God's party in 5:56 and 58:22."}, {"id": "2:258/q62/p2", "position": "It primarily evidences the preceding claim that unbelievers' guardians are false powers; later stories display God's guardianship of believers.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this alternative sequencing."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q63", "question": "How do the three adjacent stories fit together?", "turns_on": "The thematic and syntactic relation among 2:258–260.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q63/p1", "position": "They successively display the Creator's power, resurrection, and guidance through argument or witnessed signs.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the first proves the Creator and the second resurrection; Biqāʿī relates 2:243 and the ruined town; Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows three examples or three grades of guidance."}, {"id": "2:258/q63/p2", "position": "The Nimrod and passerby accounts are coordinated through 'have you seen someone like', with the comparison understood.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Thaʿlabī, Qurtubī, Burhān, and Bursevī use 2:259 to explain the continuation; some Basrans make kāf extra."}, {"id": "2:258/q63/p3", "position": "The varying dialogue forms stimulate attention and allow each story's distinct contextual effect.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes the succession of rhetorical patterns; Abū Ḥayyān says repeated qāla clauses can omit conjunction when meaning itself connects them."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q64", "question": "What connection does the verse have with Abraham's other Qur'anic arguments?", "turns_on": "Which Abraham passages are used as parallels.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q64/p1", "position": "God had given Abraham this argument against his people, as 6:83 says.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī links the debate to 6:83; Abū Ḥayyān's and Qurtubī's discussions place it among Abraham's disputes."}, {"id": "2:258/q64/p2", "position": "The episode's proof of divine unity and creation connects to Abraham's account of the sun in 6:78.", "reasons": "Study Quran notes the other rising-sun context; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says Abraham used a less abstract proof here than his own earlier insight at 6:79."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q65", "question": "What does the verse imply about God's support and the believer's conduct before a tyrant?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q65/p1", "position": "A believer should answer a false divine claim clearly and rely on God; Abraham's composure and victory demonstrate divine favor.", "reasons": "Elmalılı contrasts Abraham with people who tremble before tyrants and calls the concise debate a model; Ālūsī says the opening consoles Muhammad by recalling God's aid."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q66", "question": "Why are the three stories ordered with this one first?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q66/p1", "position": "The Nimrod story is immediately paired with its referent, foregrounds an astonishing self-contained encounter, and leaves later detailed narratives together.", "reasons": "Ālūsī gives these reasons for the order."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q67", "question": "What does the account show about Qur'anic dialectic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q67/p1", "position": "The Qur'an uses premises, conclusions, counterargument, and transitions when an opponent evades a proof.", "reasons": "Itqān points to Abraham's debate with Nimrod and his people; a subsequent entry calls the shift to sunrise intiqāl."}]}

{"id": "2:258/q69", "question": "What ancillary point does al-Farrāʾ make about replies to questions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q69/p1", "position": "A response can supply the answer after a question without repeating its opening wording.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ cites questions about ownership of earth and rule of heavens at 23:84–87."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q70", "question": "What does Wahb's ancillary account say of David and Saul?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q70/p1", "position": "David killed Goliath, delivered 300 enemy foreskins to marry Saul's daughter, and later spared Saul despite persecution; Samuel, not Saul, received revelation.", "reasons": "Wahb says David took Saul's vessel, beard hairs, and clothing fringe as proof he could have killed him; Saul later plotted again."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q71", "question": "What ancillary morphology is given for ḥāniya?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q71/p1", "position": "Ḥāna is shortened from ḥāniya on the fāʿila pattern, like bāla from bāliya.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī also cites al-Kisāʾī's derivation of āya from āyiya."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q72", "question": "How does an ancillary poetic metaphor differ from an omitted comparison?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q72/p1", "position": "The she-camel metaphor imagines qualities fully embodied and gains force from expansive hyperbole.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir rejects reducing it to an omitted mithl before moon, willow, amber, and gazelle, or treating the full paraphrase as the poem's actual composition."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q73", "question": "What ancillary principle governs word order and unity of expression?", "turns_on": "Whether thought's grammatical relations or imagined inner wording determines expression.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q73/p1", "position": "Arrangement and unity arise from grammatical and intelligible relations among meanings, not from a bare ordering or fusion of words.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir analyzes 'qifā nabki' by governing and coordination and Bashshār's line by subject, attached phrase, predication and qualification; meter is outside the argument."}, {"id": "2:258/q73/p2", "position": "Mentally picturing inner speech does not prove that thought consists of words.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir compares mentally picturing a seen object with actually seeing it."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q74", "question": "What ancillary distinction does al-Rāzī draw about God's speech and the recited Qur'an?", "turns_on": "Whether created sounds are God's eternal attribute itself or signify that attribute.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q74/p1", "position": "The eternal speech is an attribute of God; successive recited letters and sounds are created expressions signifying it.", "reasons": "Rāzī says Qur'anic miracle, sūras, verses, eloquence, and interpretation concern the expressed letters; customary oaths follow common speech usage. Denying recited Qur'an as God's speech opposes mass-transmitted religion, but identifying human sounds with the attribute would put it in a human body."}, {"id": "2:258/q74/p2", "position": "The Ḥashwiyya identify sounds heard from humans with God's own speech.", "reasons": "Rāzī rejects this and compares it to extending the Christian claim about the divine Word in Jesus to every speaking person."}, {"id": "2:258/q74/p3", "position": "Two other arguments for an uncreated audible expression fail: one would make everything eternal and another is too obscure to overcome evident facts.", "reasons": "Rāzī gives these replies in his excursus."}]}
{"id": "2:258/q75", "question": "What ancillary data does Nashr give about reading transmission?", "turns_on": "The transmitted basis and scale of the reading tradition.", "positions": [{"id": "2:258/q75/p1", "position": "Recitation is received through transmitted routes, preserving both rare and sound readings.", "reasons": "Nashr says predecessors treated recitation as transmitted Sunnah; the exceptions criticized were Ibn Shunbudh for departing from the ʿUthmānī codex and Ibn Miqsam for accepting unattested readings merely fitting the script."}, {"id": "2:258/q75/p2", "position": "Early and later reading compilations varied widely in the number of readings and routes they recorded.", "reasons": "Nashr cites an unnamed seven-reading work over 500 routes, al-Hudhalī's 50 readings and 1,459 routes from 365 teachers, al-Ṭabarī of Mecca's 1,550 routes, and al-Iskandarī's 7,000."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q01", "question": "Who is the person in hardship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q01/p1", "position": "A debtor pursued for payment, especially one whose principal remains due after usury is cancelled.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the person sought for payment; Jishumī supplies 'among your debtors' as the understood complement. Ibn ʿĀshūr says dhū can be annexed to an unfavorable quality."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q02", "question": "What does hardship mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q02/p1", "position": "Poverty or restricted access to money that prevents paying a debt.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī calls it poverty, constraint and hardship; Rāzī stresses inability to find available money; Jishumī defines ʿusra and iʿsār as little money. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites 9:117."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q03", "question": "How is ʿusra read?", "turns_on": "The sīn's vowel differs by Arabic dialect without changing the basic sense.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q03/p1", "position": "With ḍamma on sīn, attributed chiefly to Abū Jaʿfar.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and al-Nashr transmit it; al-Nashr also connects Abū ʿAmr's ḍamma of related ʿusr/yusr forms."}, {"id": "2:280/q03/p2", "position": "With sukūn on sīn, the common reading.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabrisī say both vocalizations are Arabic; Qiraat-ER says the vowel difference leaves the sense intact."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q04", "question": "How does kāna govern dhū ʿusratin?", "turns_on": "Whether kāna itself supplies existence or requires an understood predicate; the implications claimed for scope and insolvency.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q04/p1", "position": "Kāna is complete, meaning an insolvent person exists, occurs, or appears; dhū is its nominative subject.", "reasons": "Sībawayh's verse and poetry about a cloudy day or arriving winter illustrate existential kāna. Naḥḥās says this gives general scope; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say the construction presents insolvency as a state needing proof. Rāzī prefers it because a buyer-specific parse would narrow the rule. Samarrai cites poetry for occurrence and existence."}, {"id": "2:280/q04/p2", "position": "Kāna is defective with an unspoken predicate such as 'one of your debtors' or 'owing you a right.'", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says Arabic may omit a predicate with an indefinite subject; Jishumī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī and al-Samīn supply creditor–debtor relations. Al-Suyūṭī lists continuous divine attributes and Abū Bakr al-Rāzī's five temporal senses."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q05", "question": "What alternative readings recast the insolvent person?", "turns_on": "Which codex or transmitter supplies the wording and whether its implied debtor affects scope.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q05/p1", "position": "Accusative dhā ʿusratin implies a debtor as kāna's subject.", "reasons": "Attributed variously to Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUthmān and ʿAbd Allāh; Abān adds 'man' or 'wa-man'; a report adds 'for this crop.' Some infer a narrower usury context, which Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn dispute."}, {"id": "2:280/q05/p2", "position": "A reading says 'if he is insolvent' with muʿsiran.", "reasons": "Al-Aʿmash transmits it; al-Dānī reports a codex route. Thaʿlabī says it supports the received meaning. The implicit pronoun points back to the debtor."}, {"id": "2:280/q05/p3", "position": "Some codex reports substitute or add conditional particles, including wa-man and fa-in.", "reasons": "Abān is reported with wa-man; al-Mahdawī reports an ʿUthmānic fa-in. These variants variously identify an individual debtor."}, {"id": "2:280/q05/p4", "position": "The received nominative dhū ʿusratin reads an indefinite person in hardship.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī refuses Ubayy's accusative as recitation because it conflicts with written codices; al-Samīn says the majority retain nominative and Makkī takes it generally. Some commentators disagree that these readings must differ in legal scope."}, {"id": "2:280/q05/p5", "position": "Anomalous forms may explain the verse without functioning as valid recitation.", "reasons": "Jishumī explicitly treats them as explanatory paraphrases even when Arabic permits them."}]}
